newsitem.title: USA: Chase, Citicorp say earnings rose in quarter.
newsitem.headline: Chase, Citicorp say earnings rose in quarter.

text.p: Chase Manhattan Corp. and Citicorp, the nation's two largest banks, said on Tuesday that their earnings rose in the second quarter despite weakness in credit card and consumer banking operations.
Wells Fargo & Co., the No. 9 bank, said its earnings fell 37 percent, hurt by costs from completing its merger with First Interstate and higher provisions for loan losses.
The results, similar to those reported by Nationsbank, First Chicago NBD Corp. and other big banks on Monday, met or slightly exceeded expectations on Wall Street.

Chase, which took over the No. 1 spot from Citicorp when it acquired Chemical Bank last year, said net income rose to $925 million, or $2 a share, in the quarter ended on June 30, compared with $856 million, or $1.83 a share, a year earlier.

Chase, based in New York, cited strength in its corporate business worldwide and a rise in revenue from trading for its own account, partly offset by weakness in its consumer operations, where earnings declined.

Excluding restructuring costs from the Chemical merger, Chase earnings were $969 million, or $2.11 a share, which was above the $2.07 a share analysts had forecast, according to First Call, which tracks estimates.
Chase stock rose 69 cents to $102.69 in consolidated morning trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Citicorp, also based in New York, said earnings rose to $1 billion in the quarter from $952 million a year earlier, while earnings per share increased to $2.10 from $1.86.
The results were a penny above analysts' forecast of $2.09 a share, according to First Call, but Citicorp stock fell $2.31 to $126.19 on the NYSE.

The company's consumer banking business remained under pressure, and Chairman John Reed said its domestic credit card business presented "challenges." Reed also said competition had caused the spread between its cost of funds and the interest rates it can charge customers to narrow.
"Our assumption is that the highly competitive marketplace is a permanent reality," Reed said, adding that Citicorp would focus on improving customer service and cutting costs.

Earnings in Citicorp's global consumer banking and credit card business fell to $471 million from $486 million in the 1996 quarter. Corporate banking earnings rose 5 percent to $665 million in the quarter from $636 million a year earlier.

Wells Fargo, based in San Francisco, said net income fell to $228 million, or $2.49 a share, in the quarter, from $363 million, or $3.61 a share, a year earlier. The results were below forecasts of $2.52 a share, according to First Call, but Wells Fargo stock rose $1.50 to $267 on the NYSE.
"The earnings we reported this morning are clearly a disappointment for shareholders, employees and the senior management of this company," Chairman Paul Hazen said in a statement.
The company said it had higher operating losses from integrating the operations and back-office functions of First Interstate, which it acquired last year for about $11 billion in stock.
